facts.fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
facts.hook: A kid keeps opening the fridge in the dark to look for a snack until an older sibling suggests everyone decide first and open it only once.

facts.fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
facts.hook: During a long outage, a family works out whether the frozen food will last, since the freezer was only half full that week.

facts.fact: USDA guidance says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) or below.
facts.hook: When the lights come back, a boy checks a bag of frozen peas for ice crystals before the family decides whether to throw it out.

facts.fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
facts.hook: A grandparent reaches for candles, and the grandchild offers the flashlights from the kitchen drawer instead, remembering a fire-safety lesson.

facts.fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
facts.hook: At a farmhouse, a teen notices an adult about to start the generator in the garage and speaks up about running it outside.

facts.fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
facts.hook: Before bed, a girl goes around unplugging the gaming console and the desktop computer so they are not hit by a surge.

facts.fact: A fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported.
facts.hook: Walking home after the storm, two friends spot a wire across the sidewalk and turn back to tell an adult to report it.

facts.fact: A traditional corded phone on a copper landline usually keeps working in a power cut, because the phone company powers the line, but cordless phones need household electricity.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, the cordless phone is dead, and a kid finds the old wall phone in the kitchen still has a dial tone.

facts.fact: In the dark, the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more.
facts.hook: After the lights go out, a boy can barely see his hand, but half an hour later he can make out the furniture in the living room.

facts.fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
facts.hook: With the whole street dark, a family steps outside and sees far more stars than usual, and a kid wonders why.

facts.fact: The Northeast blackout that began on August 14, 2003, cut power to about 55 million people in parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario, Canada.
facts.hook: Sitting in the dark, a grandparent tells the kids about walking home from work during a huge blackout years ago.

facts.fact: A phone's bright screen is one of its biggest drains on the battery, so dimming it and closing unused apps helps a charge last longer during an outage.
facts.hook: With her phone low and no way to charge it, a girl turns down the brightness and saves the battery for a call to her mom.

facts.fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
facts.hook: A student notices an ad saying "join the millions who already switched" and asks what the product actually does better.

facts.fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda.
facts.hook: A library research project about wartime posters leads a student to a 1930s group that tried to teach ordinary people to spot propaganda.

facts.fact: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis named seven common devices: name-calling, glittering generalities, transfer, testimonial, plain folks, card stacking and bandwagon.
facts.hook: Two friends turn a pile of junk mail into a game of labeling each flyer with one of the seven devices.

facts.fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
facts.hook: A boy wants a pair of sneakers because a basketball star wears them, then wonders whether the star even chose them.

facts.fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
facts.hook: Scrolling a video review, a girl spots "#ad" in the caption and rethinks how much to trust the glowing review.

facts.fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
facts.hook: During a class news project, two students compare two headlines about the same event and notice how the word choice changes their reaction.

facts.fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
facts.hook: A kid reads "all-natural goodness" on a cereal box and flips it over to see what the ingredient list actually says.

facts.fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
facts.hook: A student sees a tablet ad listing five great features and goes looking for what the ad left out, like battery life.

facts.fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
facts.hook: During a school election, a candidate's poster shows him eating lunch in the cafeteria, and a classmate asks what his actual plan is.

facts.fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
facts.hook: A girl realizes she believes a rumor mostly because she has heard it five times, not because anyone showed proof.

facts.fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
facts.hook: Looking up word histories for a vocabulary assignment, a student is surprised by where "propaganda" comes from.

facts.fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
facts.hook: At a museum exhibit on World War II, a class stops at a display of posters made by a government propaganda ministry.

facts.fact: According to the NHS, it is normal for puberty to begin at any age between 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys.
facts.hook: A boy worries because his best friend has already shot up in height, and a doctor explains how wide the normal range is.

facts.fact: Puberty begins when the pituitary gland at the base of the brain releases hormones that signal the ovaries or testes to make more sex hormones.
facts.hook: After a health class, a girl asks her aunt, a nurse, what actually starts puberty, and hears about a gland in the brain.

facts.fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
facts.hook: A boy's shoes stop fitting twice in one school year, even though his jeans still fit fine.

facts.fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
facts.hook: During choir practice, a boy's voice cracks on a high note, and the music teacher explains why it is happening.

facts.fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
facts.hook: At a pharmacy, a girl compares face washes and reads the labels to understand why pimples started showing up this year.

facts.fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
facts.hook: After gym class, a boy wonders why he never used to need deodorant, and an older cousin explains what changed.

facts.fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
facts.hook: Standing in the store aisle, a kid has to choose between two products and reads the labels to see which one does what.

facts.fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
facts.hook: At a friend's house, two girls talk about how their older sisters got their first periods at quite different ages.

facts.fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
facts.hook: At the doctor's office, a boy asks whether he will keep growing, and the doctor points out his growth plates on an X-ray.

facts.fact: On average, girls start their pubertal growth spurt about two years earlier than boys, which is why many girls are taller than boys their age in early middle school.
facts.hook: At the class photo, the girls in the back row are taller than most of the boys, and the kids joke about why.

facts.fact: The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.
facts.hook: After an impulsive choice, a teen reads that the brain's planning region is still developing and thinks about what that means.

facts.fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
facts.hook: A girl notices faint lines on her hips and worries, until her mom mentions they are common during growth spurts.

facts.fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
facts.hook: At a grandparent's house, a kid helps line up the diyas along the window ledge before dark, with an adult lighting them.

facts.fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
facts.hook: A boy's family visits relatives on Eid morning after a month of fasting, and his friend from school comes along for the first time.

facts.fact: The Islamic calendar follows the moon and is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan starts about 11 days earlier each year.
facts.hook: A girl notices that Ramadan fell in summer when she was little but now comes in spring, and asks her grandmother why.

facts.fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
facts.hook: A kid tries to plan a school project around the family's Lunar New Year dinner and discovers the date moves every year.

facts.fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
facts.hook: The youngest cousin at the table practices the Four Questions all week and is nervous about reading them aloud.

facts.fact: A Hanukkah menorah, or hanukkiah, has nine branches: eight for the eight nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others.
facts.hook: A visiting friend asks why the menorah has nine candles when Hanukkah lasts eight nights.

facts.fact: Sikh gurdwaras serve langar, a free communal meal offered to every visitor regardless of religion, often with everyone seated together on the floor.
facts.hook: At a gurdwara, a boy's friend is surprised he can eat a meal without paying and helps serve roti afterward.

facts.fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
facts.hook: During a Vaisakhi procession, a kid asks her uncle why this day matters and hears the story of the Khalsa.

facts.fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
facts.hook: A girl brings her friend to a gurdwara and makes sure to lend her a scarf before they go in.

facts.fact: In Western churches, Easter falls on the first Sunday after the church's calculated full moon on or after March 21, so it can come anywhere from March 22 to April 25.
facts.hook: A family tries to plan a spring visit to grandparents and finds Easter lands on a different weekend than last year.

facts.fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
facts.hook: At a cultural center, a class helps set up an ofrenda, and a student adds a photo of her great-grandfather.

facts.fact: Kwanzaa, created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga, celebrates African American heritage from December 26 to January 1, with each day devoted to one of seven principles.
facts.hook: At a family gathering, a boy is asked to light the candle for the day's principle and has to explain what it means.

facts.fact: Tempo in music is measured in beats per minute, and much pop and house dance music falls roughly between 120 and 130 beats per minute.
facts.hook: Nervous about dancing, a boy practices by tapping his foot to songs on his playlist to find the beat.

facts.fact: In a 2000 study by Thomas Gilovich, students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half the room noticed it, but only about a quarter actually did.
facts.hook: Worried everyone will stare at her new outfit, a girl remembers that most classmates are busy worrying about themselves.

facts.fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
facts.hook: In the car on the way to the dance, a boy's stomach flips and his heart races before he even walks in.

facts.fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
facts.hook: At the dance, a friend cracks a glow stick bracelet, and another kid wonders where the light is coming from.

facts.fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
facts.hook: After the dance, a girl puts her glow stick in the freezer to see if it will still be glowing in the morning.

facts.fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
facts.hook: Standing next to the giant speakers, two friends move farther away when their ears start to feel strange.

facts.fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
facts.hook: The morning after the dance, a boy's ears are still ringing, and he decides to stand farther from the DJ next time.

facts.fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
facts.hook: A shy dancer watches a video of a dancing cockatoo and decides that if a bird can keep the beat, she can too.

facts.fact: The word "prom" is short for "promenade," and it names a formal dance held for high school students.
facts.hook: Planning outfits in a family group chat, a kid argues with an older cousin about whether a middle school dance counts as a prom.

facts.fact: Sweat cools the body because evaporating water carries heat away from the skin, and it works less well in a hot, humid, crowded room.
facts.hook: In the packed gym, a girl steps into the hallway with her water bottle to cool off after several fast songs.

facts.fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
facts.hook: A boy with no one to dance with joins a line dance and finds he only needs to learn a few steps.

facts.fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
facts.hook: Standing by the wall, a girl watches the spots of light sweep across the gym and figures out where they come from.

facts.fact: The Smithsonian Institution was created by an act of Congress in 1846, using money left by British scientist James Smithson, who never visited the United States in his lifetime.
facts.hook: On a museum trip, a student reads a plaque about the founder and wonders why an Englishman paid for an American museum.

facts.fact: Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, which is why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms.
facts.hook: In a dark gallery, a student complains she can barely see an old quilt until a guide explains why the lights are low.

facts.fact: Museums control temperature and humidity because changes make wood, paper and canvas swell and shrink, which can crack or warp old objects.
facts.hook: A student notices a humidity gauge in a display case and asks the guide what it is for.

facts.fact: Many museums ask visitors not to touch objects, because oils and salts from skin build up over time and can stain or damage the surfaces.
facts.hook: On a historic site tour, a boy almost runs his hand along an old wooden desk, and a classmate stops him and explains why.

facts.fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
facts.hook: At a fire station visit, a firefighter asks the class to guess why stations once had poles instead of stairs.

facts.fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
facts.hook: At the fire station, a student asks why a painting of a spotted dog hangs by the old engine.

facts.fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
facts.hook: During a fire station demonstration, the class practices crawling low under a haze from a harmless smoke machine.

facts.fact: If clothes catch fire, the safety rule is stop, drop and roll, because running feeds the flames more oxygen.
facts.hook: A firefighter picks a volunteer from the class to show stop, drop and roll on a mat.

facts.fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
facts.hook: On a farm trip, the class watches a cow chewing slowly without eating anything new and asks what it is doing.

facts.fact: A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf.
facts.hook: At a dairy farm, a student is surprised to learn that every cow in the milking barn has had a calf.

facts.fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
facts.hook: A kid collecting eggs on a farm trip asks if the eggs will hatch, since he doesn't see a rooster anywhere.

facts.fact: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days.
facts.hook: On a hot farm visit, a student thinks the pigs are just dirty until the farmer explains the mud.

facts.fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
facts.hook: A student testing paper airplanes must decide whether she is changing the wing shape or measuring the distance.

facts.fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
facts.hook: A kid's plant experiment falls apart when he realizes one pot sat by the window and the other did not.

facts.fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
facts.hook: Testing fertilizer on bean plants, a student adds one plant that gets only plain water.

facts.fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
facts.hook: A girl's first launch of her model catapult goes wildly far, so she runs it ten times before trusting the number.

facts.fact: A useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong; it is often written as "If... then..."
facts.hook: A student's first idea, "music is good for plants," gets rewritten into a prediction she can actually test.

facts.fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
facts.hook: At the kitchen table the night before the fair, a boy redraws his graph after realizing his axes are swapped.

facts.fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
facts.hook: For a taste test of name-brand versus store-brand cereal, a girl hides the boxes and labels the bowls A and B.

facts.fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
facts.hook: A boy panics when his results prove his prediction wrong, and his teacher tells him to present them anyway.

facts.fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
facts.hook: A student finds that kids who eat breakfast get better grades and has to figure out whether breakfast is the cause.

facts.fact: The first National Science Fair was held in Philadelphia in 1950 by Science Service, and it grew into today's International Science and Engineering Fair.
facts.hook: At the library, a student researching science fair history finds that the first national fair had only 30 finalists.

facts.fact: Large science fairs such as ISEF require approval from a review committee before a project uses human participants, vertebrate animals or hazardous chemicals.
facts.hook: A girl wants to survey classmates for her project and learns she needs approval forms signed before she starts.

facts.fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
facts.hook: A boy wants more than a plain volcano, so he measures how different amounts of vinegar change the eruption.

facts.fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12.
facts.hook: At a sleepover, the friends plan to stay up all night, then one of them remembers the soccer game the next morning.

facts.fact: Feeling homesick while away from home is very common; nearly everyone misses something about home when they are away.
facts.hook: Lying awake in a friend's house, a girl feels homesick and is relieved when her friend admits she felt the same at camp.

facts.fact: Sleep runs in cycles of roughly 90 minutes, and the most vivid dreams usually happen during rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep.
facts.hook: At breakfast, the friends compare the weird dreams they had and wonder why they remember some but not others.

facts.fact: Sleepwalking is more common in children than in adults, and most children who sleepwalk outgrow it.
facts.hook: A kid wakes to find his friend walking toward the door with his eyes open and gently guides him back to bed.

facts.fact: A sleeping pad keeps someone warm in a tent because the cold ground pulls heat away from the body faster than the air does.
facts.hook: In a backyard tent, a boy shivers on the bare floor until his friend's dad hands out foam pads.

facts.fact: Since January 1, 2023, U.S. law has listed nine major food allergens, including peanuts, milk, eggs and sesame, which must be declared on packaged food labels.
facts.hook: Before ordering pizza, a host parent asks whether anyone has food allergies, and a guest checks the label on the snacks.

facts.fact: Popcorn pops because water inside each kernel turns to steam when heated, building pressure until the hard hull bursts.
facts.hook: Making popcorn with a parent late at night, the friends notice a handful of kernels that never popped and wonder why.

facts.fact: Snoring happens when relaxed tissues in the throat vibrate as air passes through them during sleep.
facts.hook: One friend snores so loudly that the others move their sleeping bags to the far side of the room.

facts.fact: Yawning is contagious: seeing someone else yawn often makes people yawn too.
facts.hook: Late at night, one friend yawns and within a minute everyone in the room is yawning.

facts.fact: Sleep talking is common in children and usually harmless, and sleep talkers normally have no memory of it the next morning.
facts.hook: The next morning, a girl insists she didn't talk in her sleep, but her friends quote what she mumbled.

facts.fact: Bright screens late at night can delay sleep, because light, especially blue light, signals the brain to hold back the sleep hormone melatonin.
facts.hook: After hours of videos on a tablet, the friends can't fall asleep even after the lights go out.

facts.fact: A scary story can set off a real fear response, with a racing heart and faster breathing, even when the listener knows it is made up.
facts.hook: After a ghost story in the dark, a boy jumps at a creak on the stairs and laughs when it is just the family cat.

facts.fact: Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms, because water molecules link together in a six-sided pattern when they freeze.
facts.hook: Catching flakes on a dark mitten, a girl counts the arms on each one and finds they all have six.

facts.fact: Wilson Bentley, a farmer from Jericho, Vermont, took the first known photograph of a single snowflake on January 15, 1885.
facts.hook: Stuck inside, a boy finds old snowflake photos online and learns they were taken by a farmer over a century ago.

facts.fact: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator; some small animals survive winter in tunnels under the snow.
facts.hook: Building a snow fort, two friends notice it feels less cold inside, out of the wind.

facts.fact: Snow looks white because its many clear ice crystals scatter and reflect all colors of light in every direction.
facts.hook: Staring out the window, a kid wonders how clear ice can make a white yard.

facts.fact: Salt melts ice by lowering the temperature at which water freezes, but ordinary rock salt stops working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius (14 degrees Fahrenheit).
facts.hook: Helping shovel the front steps, a girl notices yesterday's salt isn't melting anything on a bitterly cold morning.

facts.fact: Fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite.
facts.hook: After an hour on the sledding hill, a boy's ears are numb, and his friend insists they go inside to warm up.

facts.fact: Wind makes cold air feel colder because it carries heat away from the skin faster, which is what the wind chill number describes.
facts.hook: A kid checks the weather app and sees the wind chill is far colder than the actual temperature.

facts.fact: A common rule of thumb is that about 10 inches of snow melts down to 1 inch of water, but the ratio varies widely between wet and dry snow.
facts.hook: Two kids compare shoveling this snow with last week's and wonder why this batch is so much heavier.

facts.fact: Wet snow near the freezing point packs into snowballs well because it holds a thin layer of liquid water, while very cold, dry snow crumbles.
facts.hook: Two friends try to build a snowman, but the powder won't stick together, so they wait for the afternoon sun.

facts.fact: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children under 12 be supervised while sledding and that sledding slopes be gentle and away from trees and roads.
facts.hook: At the sledding hill, a group picks the gentle slope away from the road instead of the steep one near the trees.

facts.fact: Snow squeaks underfoot when it is very cold, because the hard ice crystals rub and break instead of melting slightly under pressure.
facts.hook: Walking to a neighbor's house on a frigid morning, a kid notices every step makes a crunching squeak.

facts.fact: Shoveling heavy snow is hard work for the heart, so doctors advise taking breaks and lifting small loads rather than big shovelfuls.
facts.hook: A girl helps an older neighbor clear the driveway and suggests they take turns and rest between rows.

facts.fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
facts.hook: A kid argues his favorite player is underrated because the batting average ignores all the times he got on base by a walk.

facts.fact: Ted Williams batted .406 in 1941 and is the last Major League Baseball player to finish a season above .400.
facts.hook: At a baseball game, a grandparent bets the grandkid that no one has hit .400 since before the grandparent was born.

facts.fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
facts.hook: Comparing players on a computer, a kid is baffled that one player wins each season but loses when the seasons are added together.

facts.fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
facts.hook: A girl's teammate brags about a perfect shooting percentage after taking a single shot all season.

facts.fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
facts.hook: A kid reads two news stories about the same poll and can't understand why one says 10 and the other says 25.

facts.fact: In ice hockey, a player's plus-minus goes up by one when their team scores while they are on the ice and down by one when the other team does; power-play goals do not count.
facts.hook: At a hockey rink, a kid wonders why a star player has a negative plus-minus even though he scored twice this week.

facts.fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
facts.hook: Watching a race on TV, the family sees the silver medalist lose by less than a blink.

facts.fact: The International Olympic Committee orders medal tables by gold medals first, while most U.S. newspapers rank countries by total medals, so the "top" country can differ.
facts.hook: A family argues about which country won the Olympics, and each side is using a different medal table.

facts.fact: An unusually great performance tends to be followed by a more ordinary one, a pattern called regression to the mean, popularized by Francis Galton in the late 1800s.
facts.hook: A kid is sure his team's star is in a slump, until his older sister points out his hot streak was never typical.

facts.fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
facts.hook: At a sports bar with family, an uncle explains how a low-budget team used numbers to compete with rich teams.

facts.fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
facts.hook: A kid on the couch asks why a "perfect" passer rating is such a strange number instead of 100.

facts.fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
facts.hook: Picking a teammate for a tournament, two friends compare players with the same average but very different game-by-game records.
